newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street not yet alarmed by rise in dollar.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street not yet alarmed by rise in dollar.

text.p: A further rise in the U.S. dollar will take a bite out of corporate earnings, but the currency has yet to reach levels that cause anxiety on Wall Street.
For the time being, short-term benefits of the strong dollar attracting foreign investors to U.S. securities are outweighing concerns over its impact on corporate profits, analysts said on Tuesday.
"It's an issue, it's out on the radar screen, but it's not flashing red at this point," said Charlie Crane, chief market strategist at Key Asset Management.

The dollar on Tuesday drove above 1.80 marks for the first time in nearly six years, but finished the day lower after German officials said the dollar had risen too far. The U.S. currency has gained amid signs Europe's proposed single currency will be weak. The dollar rose Tuesday against the Japanese yen after a Japanese official said the market was too optimistic about the yen.
The stronger dollar could impact U.S. corporations' foreign earnings by diminishing overseas sales when they are translated back into dollars.
But the surging greenback has yet to trip up Wall Street's bull run. On Tuesday, the Dow industrials closed at a record high, jumping 52.73 points to 7975.71.
Analysts noted that improvement in overseas economies, particularily in Europe, will lead to greater local sales by U.S. companies, potentially offsetting currency losses.
Efforts by U.S. companies to streamline their operations is also a factor in keeping them competitive, despite the disadvantages of a stronger dollar.
"The dollar has not risen enough to change the competitiveness that many of the companies have gained over the years," Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney.
Companies have also developed sophisticated currency hedging programs to keep currency fluctuations from doing major damage to their bottom lines, analysts said.
"Multinational earnings have not been affected in the last four quarters anywhere near the extent I think any of us had thought," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany.
The strong dollar has also made U.S. Treasuries and stocks attractive to foreign investors, analysts said.
"The stronger dollar is a double-edged sword," said Gail Dudack, chief investment strategist UBS Securities.
"It hurts multinational earnings, but since foreign investors are still relatively underowned in U.S. markets, a market with a strong currency is attractive for money managers."

The Federal Reserve has estimated that in the first quarter foreigners bought U.S. stocks at twice the pace of last year, accounting for 6.5 percent of the more than $10.1 trillion invested in the U.S. stock market.
Johnson expected policy makers to take action to stem the rise of the dollar when signs emerge that U.S. manufacturers are losing competitive edge in the United States to cheaper foreign imports.
"It perhaps hasn't become painful yet, but sooner or later it becomes painful because it hurts business for domestic manufacturers," Johnson said.
